articles.title: Llama 4 vs Mistral Large vs Qwen 3: Open-Weight LLMs Head to Head
articles.excerpt: The open-source LLM landscape in 2026 is unrecognizable from just two years ago. Meta's Llama 4, Mistral's Large model, and Alibaba's Qwen 3 now rival — and in some cases surpass — proprietary models…
articles.body: The open-source LLM landscape in 2026 is unrecognizable from just two years ago. Meta's Llama 4, Mistral's Large model, and Alibaba's Qwen 3 now rival — and in some cases surpass — proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic. But which one should you build on? The decision across coding, reasoning, multilingual tasks, and creative writing comes down to which open-source LLM deserves your compute budget in 2026. Quick Verdict Llama 4 is the best all-around choice with the largest ecosystem, best fine-tuning support, and strong performance across all tasks. Mistral Large excels at reasoning and coding with its mixture-of-experts architecture that delivers frontier performance at lower compute cost.

articles.title: A 28-Character String Freezes Your Regex for 3.6 Seconds
articles.excerpt: Your test suite passes, staging passes, and then one user submits a 28-character string and a Node process pins a core for 3.6 seconds. I measured this today on Node 22 (V8) with /^(a+)+$/ against an…
articles.body: Your test suite passes, staging passes, and then one user submits a 28-character string and a Node process pins a core for 3.6 seconds. I measured this today on Node 22 (V8) with /^(a+)+$/ against an input of n letters a followed by a single X that makes the match fail: input result time 20 chars no match 8.6 ms 22 chars no match 34.2 ms 24 chars no match 136.6 ms 26 chars no match 553.7 ms 27 chars no match 1,103.8 ms 28 chars no match 3,586.4 ms Every extra character doubles the work. Twelve more characters is 2^12 = 4,096x, so the same 40-character input would take roughly four hours. The same pattern against 'a'.repeat(5000) with no trailing X returns a match in 0 ms . That is the whole trap: catastrophic backtracking only fires when the match fails . Happy-path tests never touch it.

articles.title: How to Diagnose DKIM Failures After an NS Migration
articles.excerpt: 📝 Originally published (in Japanese) at forge.workstyle.tech. TL;DR After an NS migration, mail was delivered but DKIM failed four days later. SPF passed, and the DMARC policy was p=none. Comparing a…
articles.body: 📝 Originally published (in Japanese) at forge.workstyle.tech . TL;DR After an NS migration, mail was delivered but DKIM failed four days later. SPF passed, and the DMARC policy was p=none . Comparing all records with dig showed that the new DNS was missing one DKIM TXT record. TL;DR After migrating nameservers, DKIM was failing because the new DNS was missing a TXT record used by the mail server for DKIM. Before removing the old DNS, I compared all the records, added the missing one, and confirmed DKIM=pass with a sending test. DKIM was still failing even though SPF passed and DMARC was set to p=none . Why Was Only DKIM Failing? Comparing all the records on the old and new DNS servers with dig , I found that the new DNS was missing only the TXT record for the mail server’s DKIM.

articles.body: Building a mobile app is exciting. You have an idea, a clear vision, and expectations about how users will interact with your product. But while most businesses focus on features, design, and launch dates, one important aspect often gets overlooked: the app's architecture. An application might work perfectly when it has 100 users. But what happens when that number grows to 10,000 or even 100,000? Slow loading times, unexpected crashes, database bottlenecks, and performance issues can quickly turn growth into a technical challenge. That's why scalability should not be something developers think about after an app becomes successful. It should be part of the development strategy from day one. 1. articles.title: Your competitor report can invent an equal-demand race
articles.excerpt: Three competitors can each hit 100 without having equal search interest. You're wiring up a competitor report. Retrieval finds a peak score for each brand, the model calls the race a tie, and every ci…
articles.body: Three competitors can each hit 100 without having equal search interest. You're wiring up a competitor report. Retrieval finds a peak score for each brand, the model calls the race a tie, and every citation points to a valid record. That's the annoying part: the evidence can be individually correct while the comparison is wrong. Lab note 053: we wanted to know where a pipeline should stop that conclusion. The main caveat comes first: independently requested terms have independently normalized scores. Putting those records in the same prompt doesn't create a shared measurement scale. Why do identical peaks invent a tie? Independent keyword requests can't support a cross-brand score ranking; that ranking needs evidence from the same shared comparison row.

articles.excerpt: The Taurid meteor shower could spawn dazzling fireballs in the coming weeks! Here's when and where to look.
articles.body: Heads up stargazers! The Taurid meteor shower is upon us, bringing multiple peaks of activity that could see spectacular shooting stars and fireballs brighten November's sky. Here's where and when to look. What is the Taurid meteor shower(s)? Every autumn, Earth plows through streams of debris left behind by Comet Encke, a 3-mile-wide (4.8-kilometer) ice body that orbits the sun once every 3.3 years. These debris streams produce two branches of the Taurid meteor shower : The Southern Taurids, active from Sept. 20 to Nov. 20 and the Northern Taurids, active from Oct. 20 to Dec. 10. As Earth plows through the debris streams, tiny particles slam into our atmosphere at 65,000 miles per hour (104,607 kilometers per hour), producing dazzling streaks of light across the night sky.

articles.title: NASA asks industry for ideas about saving Hubble Space Telescope
articles.excerpt: The Hubble Space Telescope is healthy but is being pulled down toward Earth by atmospheric drag. NASA is considering options to extend the iconic telescope's work.
articles.body: NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now. The agency issued a request for information (RFI) on Oct. 29 for "in-space servicing" capabilities, which could include boosting Hubble's orbit (which is naturally degrading due to atmospheric drag), or even a mission to "enhance its capabilities" in some way. Hubble, which launched in April 1990 in partnership with the European Space Agency , was serviced five times by astronauts on space shuttle missions, the most recent being in 2009.
